result.summary: Pausanias describes the Olympia statue of Polydamas, the huge pancratium victor from Scotusa, and recounts the destruction of his hometown. He lists Polydamas' feats, including killing a lion, holding a bull, stopping a chariot and fighting Persian Immortals, and his death when a cave roof collapsed.

scenes.title: Statue and fate of Scotusa
scenes.summary: Pausanias introduces the statue of Polydamas and tells how Alexander of Pheræ massacred the people of Scotusa.
scenes.stakes: The people of Scotusa face massacre and enslavement.

scenes.title: Feats of Polydamas
scenes.summary: Polydamas kills a lion on Mount Olympus, holds a bull by its hoof and stops a speeding chariot.
scenes.stakes: Polydamas risks death by lion, bull and chariot in demonstrating his strength.

scenes.title: Summoned to Susa
scenes.summary: King Darius lures Polydamas to Susa, where he kills three Immortals.
scenes.stakes: Polydamas faces single combat against Persian Immortals.

scenes.title: Death in the cave
scenes.summary: Polydamas tries to hold up a collapsing cave roof while his friends flee and is crushed.
scenes.stakes: Polydamas' life, lost through overconfidence in his strength.

analysis.text: Polydamas' feats imitate Hercules, but his overconfidence in strength brings his death, a warning about hubris.
Pausanias links athletes' statues at Olympia to local history, such as the destruction of Scotusa by a tyrant of Pheræ.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias dates the Scotusa massacre by the Athenian Archon and the 102nd Olympiad, showing how Greeks reckoned time.

language_notes.text: Heroes means the legendary figures of the age before the Trojan War; Pausanias allows only them or mythical giants to have been bigger.
Targeteers were soldiers armed with the light small shield called a target.
The pancratium was a combined wrestling and boxing contest with very few rules.
Commonalty means the common people, here the Persian populace who supported Darius against Sogdius.
The Immortals were the elite Persian royal guard, so called because their number was always kept at full strength.
Refers to a Homeric warning that reliance on one's own strength brings ruin; Pausanias applies it to Polydamas.

context_notes.text: Lysippus was a famous fourth-century BC sculptor from Sicyon, best known as Alexander the Great's court sculptor.
Alexander of Pheræ was a ruthless tyrant of Thessaly in the mid-fourth century BC.
Killing the Nemean lion was the first of Hercules' labours; Polydamas imitates him.
Susa was one of the main royal capitals of the Persian empire.

literary_notes.text: Imagining mythical giants as the only larger men stresses Polydamas' enormous size.
Comparing Polydamas to Hercules frames him as a heroic figure and a mortal rival of the demigod.
The warning about overconfidence prepares the reader for his fatal end in the cave.
His strength, the source of his fame, leads him to attempt the impossible and causes his death.
